Paper Title: (Why) Is My Prompt Getting Worse? Rethinking Regression Testing for Evolving LLM APIs
Authors: Wanqin Ma; Chenyang Yang; Christian Kästner
Venue / Source: CAIN 2024 (IEEE/ACM 3rd International Conference on AI Engineering – Software Engineering for AI)
Main Problem: How should regression testing be reconceived for LLM-API-backed applications, given that silent API/model updates can cause performance regressions and that traditional notions of correctness, prompting brittleness, and non-determinism break standard regression-testing assumptions?
Failure Type: Model-version regression (case study: toxicity-detection prompt regression after silent API change)
Models / Sizes: Five OpenAI GPT-3.5-family models: gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, text-davinci-003, text-davinci-002 (Table 1), studied as 10 pairwise update comparisons
Serving Stack: OpenAI API (per case-study framing; not independently confirmed line-by-line)
Tasks / Dataset: Case study: toxicity detection on Civil Comments (1,000 sampled comments) and a GitHub Discussion dataset (174 discussions); four prompt strategies (P1-P4)
Detection Method: Case-study analysis; accuracy/F1 at temperature 0; entropy-based confidence analysis (n=20, temp 0.7) to test regression location relative to decision boundary
Metrics: Accuracy; F1; prediction-flip rate; entropy-based confidence measure
Main Findings: Using a toxicity-detection case study, shows silent updates to LLM APIs can cause measurable performance regressions: 58.8% of prompt+model combinations dropped accuracy across an update (70.2% of drops exceeded 5 points); 10.9% of individual predictions flipped correct-to-wrong; 63.8% of regressions occurred at maximal model confidence (entropy=0); regressions concentrated disproportionately on toxic, political, code-targeted, and severe-toxicity discussions. Argues traditional regression testing needs fundamental changes for LLM APIs.
Limitations: Authors' own stated limitation: results should not be generalized beyond the specific prompt formats and single-turn request setup used; optimal prompt design may change under different LLM APIs. Single case study (toxicity detection); does not propose a concrete automated detection system; does not compare against infrastructure-health signals; no controlled multi-fault injection framework.
How It Relates to SemaFailBench: Foundation; Fault-Design Source. Directly motivates the "model-revision mismatch" fault category in SemaFailBench's taxonomy and supports the core premise that LLM behavior can silently regress across API/model updates in ways ordinary testing misses. Its own data-slice-level, non-determinism-aware measurement design prefigures SemaFailBench's own statistical requirements (see Spec Section 16).
Research Gap It Leaves: Establishes the problem and motivates regression testing conceptually but does not build a reusable benchmark, does not inject a range of deployment faults beyond model-version change, and does not test whether lightweight canary prompts can catch such regressions faster than ad hoc case-study analysis.

Full text (Method, Experiments, Limitations) inspected directly via arXiv HTML v2 in the third pass. Main Problem: How can developers efficiently discover and understand behavioral differences introduced by migrating an LLM-backed application between model versions, and can a purpose-built interactive tool outperform manual regression-testing workflows?

Tasks / Dataset: User study comparing RETAIN-assisted vs. manual evaluation on LLM migration tasks
Detection Method: Interactive error-discovery module generating textual descriptions of output differences; human-in-the-loop comparison
Metrics: Number of errors identified; number of prompts tested; task metric scores (exact metric names not confirmed in this pass)

Paper Title: PromptRobust: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Large Language Models on Adversarial Prompts
Authors: Kaijie Zhu; Jindong Wang; Jiaheng Zhou; Zichen Wang; Hao Chen; Yidong Wang; Linyi Yang; Wei Ye; Yue Zhang; Neil Zhenqiang Gong; Xing Xie
Venue / Source: arXiv preprint (technical report; code released as "PromptBench")
Main Problem: How robust are LLMs to adversarial, meaning-preserving perturbations of prompts (character/word/sentence/semantic level), and how transferable is this robustness across models and tasks?
Models / Sizes: Multiple contemporary open- and closed-source LLMs (exact list not confirmed in this pass)
Tasks / Dataset: Sentiment analysis; natural language inference; reading comprehension; machine translation; math problem-solving (8 tasks, 13 datasets; 4,788 adversarial prompts)
Detection Method: Task-specific scoring under adversarial prompt perturbation
Metrics: Task accuracy / performance drop (average 39% drop for word-level attacks)
Main Findings: Generated 4,788 adversarial prompts across 8 tasks/13 datasets and found contemporary LLMs are not robust to adversarial prompt perturbations, with word-level attacks causing the largest average performance drop (39%); robustness does not reliably transfer across models.
Limitations: Focuses on adversarially crafted perturbations (attacker-style) rather than benign deployment-configuration changes; no deployment/serving-fault framing; no infrastructure-health comparison; some findings may reflect prompt robustness rather than serving-layer regressions.
How It Relates to SemaFailBench: Related Method; Evaluation-Method Source. Demonstrates that small, systematic prompt/format perturbations can be used as standardized stress tests, informing the design of SemaFailBench's semantic-canary prompt suite and its sensitivity analysis across perturbation types.
Research Gap It Leaves: Evaluates prompt robustness as an intrinsic model property, not as a deployment-monitoring signal; does not test whether such perturbation sensitivity can be repurposed as a canary for detecting serving-side faults distinct from adversarial attack.
Notes: Reviewed at abstract/metadata level for this interim pass (verified via primary source listed in URL/DOI); full-text Method/Experiments/Limitations sections not yet reviewed line-by-line. arXiv:2306.04528, v1 7 Jun 2023, latest v5 16 Jul 2024. Paper Title: ChatBug: A Common Vulnerability of Aligned LLMs Induced by Chat Templates
Authors: Fengqing Jiang; Zhangchen Xu; Luyao Niu; Bill Yuchen Lin; Radha Poovendran
Venue / Source: AAAI 2025 (per arXiv comment: "accepted to AAAI 2025"; exact proceedings pagination not confirmed in this pass)
Main Problem: Does the rigid formatting imposed by chat templates create an exploitable vulnerability, since LLMs are trained to expect the template format but users are not required to follow it, and can this be leveraged to bypass safety alignment?
Models / Sizes: Eight state-of-the-art LLMs (exact identities not confirmed in this pass)
Tasks / Dataset: Safety/jailbreak evaluation using two purpose-built attacks exploiting chat-template deviation
Detection Method: Adversarial attack construction + attack-success-rate evaluation
Metrics: Attack success rate; performance degradation under adversarial-training countermeasure
Main Findings: Identifies "ChatBug," a vulnerability whereby deviating from the exact chat-template format a model was fine-tuned on can bypass safety alignment; demonstrates this against eight SOTA LLMs and shows it can amplify existing jailbreak attacks; adversarial training mitigates the vulnerability but at a cost to general helpfulness.
Limitations: Frames chat-template deviation as an attacker-controlled exploit rather than an accidental deployment misconfiguration; does not test unintentional chat-template mismatches (e.g., wrong template applied by a serving pipeline) or measure downstream task-quality degradation beyond safety bypass.
How It Relates to SemaFailBench: Fault-Design Source. Directly evidences that chat-template handling is safety- and behavior-critical, supporting SemaFailBench's inclusion of "incorrect chat templates" as a deployment fault category, though ChatBug studies adversarial exploitation rather than accidental misconfiguration.
Research Gap It Leaves: Does not test the accidental/operational case central to SemaFailBench — a serving pipeline silently applying the wrong or malformed chat template — nor does it propose a canary-based detector for such misconfigurations under normal infrastructure telemetry.
Notes: Reviewed at abstract/metadata level for this interim pass (verified via primary source listed in URL/DOI); full-text Method/Experiments/Limitations sections not yet reviewed line-by-line. arXiv:2406.12935, v1 17 Jun 2024, v2 7 Jan 2025 (post-acceptance revision). Paper Title: POSIX: A Prompt Sensitivity Index For Large Language Models
Authors: Anwoy Chatterjee; H S V N S Kowndinya Renduchintala; Sumit Bhatia; Tanmoy Chakraborty
Main Problem: How can prompt sensitivity — the degree to which an LLM's output log-likelihood changes under intent-preserving prompt rewordings — be quantified as a standardized index, and what factors (scale, instruction tuning, few-shot exemplars) modulate it?
Models / Sizes: Multiple open-source LLMs (exact list not confirmed in this pass)
Tasks / Dataset: MCQ-type tasks; open-ended generation tasks (exact dataset names not confirmed in this pass)
Detection Method: POSIX metric — relative change in response log-likelihood under intent-preserving prompt substitution
Metrics: POSIX score (log-likelihood-based sensitivity index)
Main Findings: Proposes POSIX, a log-likelihood-based prompt-sensitivity index; finds that increasing parameter count or instruction tuning alone does not reduce prompt sensitivity, while adding even one few-shot exemplar substantially reduces it; template alterations most affect MCQ tasks while paraphrasing most affects open-ended generation.
Limitations: Sensitivity is measured via log-likelihood, which requires model access not always available for closed API deployments; static evaluation rather than continuous production monitoring; no deployment-fault injection or infrastructure-signal comparison.
How It Relates to SemaFailBench: Related Method; Baseline Source. POSIX-style log-likelihood sensitivity scoring is a candidate lightweight baseline detector for chat-template and prompt-format canaries in SemaFailBench, when logit/log-likelihood access is available from the serving stack.
Research Gap It Leaves: Quantifies static prompt sensitivity as a model property; does not test whether POSIX-style scores can flag a *change* introduced by a deployment fault (e.g., an incorrectly applied chat template) relative to a known-healthy baseline.
Notes: Reviewed at abstract/metadata level for this interim pass (verified via primary source listed in URL/DOI); full-text Method/Experiments/Limitations sections not yet reviewed line-by-line. Confirmed EMNLP 2024 Findings via arXiv Comments field. arXiv:2410.02185, v1 3 Oct 2024, v2 4 Oct 2024.

Paper Title: On the Loss of Context-awareness in General Instruction Fine-tuning
Authors: Yihan Wang; Andrew Bai; Nanyun Peng; Cho-Jui Hsieh
Main Problem: Does applying a chat template during instruction fine-tuning and inference cause instruction-tuned LLMs to lose "context awareness" (the ability to use user-provided context), and if so, why?
Models / Sizes: Three pre-trained LLMs of different sizes (exact identities not confirmed in this pass)
Tasks / Dataset: Four context-dependent downstream tasks (exact names not confirmed in this pass)
Detection Method: Attention-allocation visualization; proposed context-dependency metric; conditional instruction fine-tuning intervention
Metrics: Task performance on context-dependent benchmarks (exact metric names not confirmed in this pass)
Main Findings: Shows that applying the chat template during and after instruction fine-tuning induces a measurable loss of context-awareness in open-source LLMs, traceable to attention bias toward learned conversational roles; proposes a context-dependency indicator and conditional fine-tuning method that mitigates the loss across four tasks and three model sizes.
Limitations: Studies context-awareness loss as a training-time phenomenon rather than a deployment/serving fault; does not test what happens when a chat template is applied incorrectly or inconsistently at serving time versus training time; limited to open-source models.
How It Relates to SemaFailBench: Related Method; Fault-Design Source. Provides mechanistic evidence (attention bias) for why chat-template application changes model behavior, strengthening the theoretical basis for treating chat-template faults as a distinct, detectable failure category.
Research Gap It Leaves: Does not test the training/serving-template mismatch scenario central to SemaFailBench (e.g., a template applied at inference that differs from the one used in fine-tuning), only the presence/absence of template application during fine-tuning itself.
Notes: Reviewed at abstract/metadata level for this interim pass (verified via primary source listed in URL/DOI); full-text Method/Experiments/Limitations sections not yet reviewed line-by-line. arXiv:2411.02688, v1 5 Nov 2024, v3 2 Feb 2025 (venue of eventual publication, if any, not confirmed in this pass — treated as arXiv preprint per Rule 9).

Authors: Jin Yang; Zhiqiang Wang; Yanbin Lin; Zunduo Zhao
Venue / Source: 11th IEEE Special Session on Privacy and Security of Big Data (PSBD 2024)

Paper Title: S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters
Authors: Ying Sheng; Shiyi Cao; Dacheng Li; Coleman Hooper; Nicholas Lee; Shuo Yang; Christopher Chou; Banghua Zhu; Lianmin Zheng; Kurt Keutzer; Joseph E. Gonzalez; Ion Stoica
